quizzes.title: Key terms and ideas
quizzes.intro: Ten quick checks on routes, route costs and the parts of a machine's cost per metre.

questions.q: In this lecture, what is a processing "route"?
options: The path of the fabric truck from grey store to dye house
The sequence of machines a fabric passes through to reach its shade and finish
The order in which customers are served
A list of dyes used for one shade
questions.explain: A route is the sequence of processes, such as bleaching → mercerizing → pad steam dyeing → stenter. Different sequences can give the same shade at very different cost.

questions.q: How is the cost per metre of a route found?
options: By taking the cost of the most expensive process
By adding the cost per metre of every process in the route
By multiplying the process costs together
questions.explain: Route 1 = bleaching 3.05 + mercerizing 14 + pad steam 12 + stenter 5 = Rs 34.05 per metre: a plain sum.

questions.q: Route 4 (bleaching → cold pad batch → washing) is the cheapest at Rs 13.05, but it is slower and suits reactive dyes only.
questions.explain: The lecture notes that cold pad batch ties up fabric for batching time and is limited to reactive dyes, so the cheapest route is not always the right one.

questions.q: Which process appears in every one of the five routes?
questions.explain: All five routes begin with bleaching. Mercerizing is in three routes, the stenter in three, washing in two.

questions.q: Which route is the most expensive in the lecture sheet?
options: Route 2, thermosol with washing after mercerizing
questions.explain: Route 2 = 3.05 + 14 + 12 + 4 + 5 = Rs 38.05, because thermosol needs a separate wash and still needs a stenter pass.

questions.q: The "total capital cost per year" of the bleaching range is made up of:
questions.explain: €250,000 depreciation (2.5 million ÷ 10 years) plus €250,000 financial cost (10% of machine cost) = €500,000 a year.

questions.q: In the sheet, financial cost is taken as 10% of the machine's cost every year.
questions.explain: Line 3 is machine cost × 10% = €250,000 a year, charged on the full price for each of the ten years.

questions.q: Why does the lecture say that routing is not only a cost decision?
options: Because process costs are too uncertain to compare
Because the cheapest route may be slower or limited to certain dye classes
Because buyers always specify the route
Because utilities are the same on every route
questions.explain: Cold pad batch is a third of the cost of route 2 but ties up fabric for batching and suits reactive dyes only; quality and delivery count alongside cost.

questions.q: "Effective cloth per hour" in the bleaching build-up means:
questions.explain: 130 m/min × 60 = 7,800 m/h nominal; × 80% efficiency = 6,240 m/h actually processed, the figure the capital cost is spread over.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the items in the lecture's Rs 3.05 bleaching cost build-up?
questions.explain: The build-up has capital cost, chemicals, water, air, steam and power. Labour is not included in this particular sheet (it appears in the per-minute fixed cost of Lecture 24).

quizzes.title: Formulas and relationships
quizzes.intro: How machine cost, hours, speed, efficiency and tariffs each move the cost per metre of a process.

questions.q: Depreciation per year of the bleaching range is:
questions.explain: €2,500,000 ÷ 10 years = €250,000 a year. Machine cost × 10% is the financial cost, which happens to be the same number here.

questions.q: The sheet converts the yearly capital cost to a cost per hour by dividing by:
questions.explain: €500,000 ÷ 8,760 = €57.08 per hour, assuming the continuous range runs round the clock all year.

questions.q: If the bleaching range ran at twice the speed with the same efficiency, its capital cost per metre would halve.
questions.explain: Capital cost per hour is fixed; spreading it over twice as many metres per hour halves the cost per metre (0.6516 → 0.3258).

questions.q: Efficiency falls from 80% to 60%. Capital cost per metre:
questions.explain: Effective cloth per hour falls from 6,240 to 4,680 m, so cost per metre = 4,066 ÷ 4,680 = Rs 0.869, which is 80 ÷ 60 = 1.33 times the Rs 0.652.

questions.q: Water cost per metre in the sheet is:
options: Litres per hour × Rs per litre × metres per hour
Litres per hour × Rs per litre ÷ metres per hour
Litres per metre ÷ Rs per litre
Rs per litre ÷ litres per hour
questions.explain: 4,125 litres/h × Rs 1 ÷ 7,800 m/h = Rs 0.5288 per metre. Rupees per hour must be divided by metres per hour.

questions.q: The depreciation period is shortened from 10 to 5 years. Total capital cost per year becomes:
questions.explain: Depreciation doubles to €500,000 while financial cost stays €250,000, so the total is €750,000. Only the depreciation line depends on the period.

questions.q: A weaker rupee (more rupees per euro) raises the capital cost per metre but leaves the utility costs in the sheet unchanged.
questions.explain: Only the capital cost is in euros and converted at Rs 71.238; water, air, steam and power are entered at rupee tariffs.

questions.q: Which cost per metre in the bleaching build-up is unaffected by the machine's efficiency?
questions.explain: Chemicals are entered directly at Rs 1 per metre. Capital cost per metre, and therefore the total, rise when efficiency falls.

questions.q: Route 1 costs Rs 34.05 and route 3 costs Rs 20.05. The Rs 14 difference is:
questions.explain: Route 3 is route 1 without mercerizing, and mercerizing is Rs 14 per metre in the sheet.

questions.q: If the steam tariff doubles from Rs 0.5 to Rs 1 per kg, the steam cost per metre:
questions.explain: Steam cost per metre is kg/h × Rs/kg ÷ m/h, proportional to the tariff: 5,410 × 1 ÷ 7,800 = Rs 0.694.

quizzes.title: Worked calculations
quizzes.intro: Rebuild the bleaching cost of Rs 3.05 per metre step by step, then total a route.

questions.q: A bleaching range costs €2,500,000 and is depreciated over 10 years. Depreciation per year?
Machine cost €2,500,000, depreciation 10 years, financial cost 10% of machine cost per year. Total capital cost per year?
questions.explain: Depreciation 250,000 + financial cost 250,000 = €500,000.

questions.q: Total capital cost is €500,000 a year. Spread over every hour of the year (365 × 24), what is the cost per hour, to the nearest cent?
Capital cost is €57.08 per hour and the exchange rate is Rs 71.238 per euro. Capital cost per hour in rupees, to the nearest rupee?
The range runs at 130 m/min at 80% efficiency. Effective cloth processed per hour?
questions.explain: 130 × 60 = 7,800 m/h nominal; × 0.80 = 6,240 m/h effective.

questions.q: Capital cost is Rs 4,066 per hour and the range processes 6,240 m effectively per hour. Capital cost per metre, to four decimals?
The range uses 4,125 litres of water per hour at Rs 1 per litre and runs 7,800 m per hour. Water cost per metre, to four decimals?
Steam use is 5,410 kg per hour (2,030 + 560 + 2,820) at Rs 0.5 per kg; the range runs 7,800 m per hour. Steam cost per metre, to four decimals?
Process costs per metre: bleaching 3.05, mercerizing 14, thermosol 12, washing 4, stenter 5. Cost of route 2 (bleaching → mercerizing → thermosol → washing → stenter)?
Power is 375 kW at Rs 8 per kWh and the range runs 7,800 m per hour. Power cost per metre is about:
questions.explain: 375 × 8 = Rs 3,000 per hour; ÷ 7,800 = Rs 0.3846 per metre. Rs 0.48 is what you get by dividing by the effective 6,240 m/h instead of the sheet's 7,800.

quizzes.title: Applied in practice
quizzes.intro: Choosing routes and checking process costs in a dye-house costing office.

questions.q: A customer needs a reactive-dyed shade delivered quickly and cannot wait for batching time. From the sheet's five routes, the sensible choice is:
options: Route 4, cold pad batch, at Rs 13.05
Route 3, pad steam without mercerizing, at Rs 20.05
Route 2, thermosol with washing, at Rs 38.05
Route 1, pad steam after mercerizing, at Rs 34.05
questions.explain: Cold pad batch is cheapest but slow. Pad steam is continuous; route 3 gives it without the Rs 14 of mercerizing, which the customer has not asked for.

questions.q: Mercerizing adds Rs 14 per metre to a route. When is it justified?
options: Always, because it lowers dye cost
Only when the buyer's specification needs the lustre, strength or dye yield it gives
questions.explain: Mercerizing is a quality decision; the costing sheet puts a price (Rs 14) on it so that the choice is made knowingly rather than by habit.

questions.q: If the bleaching range runs at 60% efficiency instead of 80%, its capital cost per metre rises to about Rs 0.87.
questions.explain: Effective cloth = 7,800 × 0.60 = 4,680 m/h; 4,066 ÷ 4,680 = Rs 0.869 per metre.

questions.q: The mill buys a bleaching range for €3.5 million instead of €2.5 million, everything else unchanged. Capital cost per metre becomes about:
Steam from the mill's own boiler costs Rs 0.3 per kg instead of Rs 0.5. The saving on bleaching, per metre, is about:
questions.explain: 5,410 kg/h × Rs 0.2 = Rs 1,082 per hour; ÷ 7,800 m = Rs 0.139 per metre.

questions.q: Route 5 (stenter dyeing) costs Rs 25.05 against Rs 34.05 for route 1. What does stenter dyeing replace to save Rs 9?
options: Pad steam dyeing and the separate stenter pass
questions.explain: Route 1 has pad steam 12 + stenter 5 = Rs 17; route 5 replaces both with stenter dyeing at Rs 8, saving Rs 9.

questions.q: The sheet spreads the yearly capital cost over 8,760 hours. If the range actually runs 6,000 hours a year, the true capital cost per metre is:
options: Zero, because idle hours cost nothing
questions.explain: Rs per hour rises to 4,066 × 8,760 ÷ 6,000 = Rs 5,936; ÷ 6,240 = Rs 0.951. Idle hours still carry depreciation and finance.

questions.q: Running a machine on only a fraction of the plant's fabric lowers its utilisation and so raises its capital cost per metre processed.
questions.explain: Capital cost per year is fixed; fewer metres through the machine means more rupees per metre. The sheet's "fraction of fabric undergoing this process" is there for exactly this.

questions.q: A dark cotton shade is wanted in three weeks and the cold pad batch machine is idle. Which route should the costing office quote?
options: Route 2, because dark shades need thermosol
Route 4, cold pad batch, since time and dye class allow it
Route 1, because mercerizing is always needed for dark shades
Route 5, because stenter dyeing is fastest
questions.explain: With reactive dyes acceptable and delivery time comfortable, the Rs 13.05 route is the right one; the constraints that rule it out (speed, dye class) do not apply here.

questions.q: The office costs an order on route 1 at Rs 34.05 but the dye house actually runs route 2. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing, the shade is the same
The order under-recovers Rs 4 per metre of processing cost
The order over-recovers Rs 4 per metre
questions.explain: Route 2 costs Rs 38.05, so every metre costs Rs 4 more than was priced. Costing and production must agree on the route before quoting.

quizzes.title: Challenge review
quizzes.intro: Harder questions: new machines, changed tariffs and the hidden assumptions in the bleaching build-up.

questions.q: A mercerizer costs €1,800,000, is depreciated over 8 years and carries financial cost of 10% of machine cost per year. Total capital cost per year?
questions.explain: Depreciation 225,000 + financial cost 180,000 = €405,000 a year.

questions.q: That mercerizer (€405,000 a year over 8,760 hours) runs at 100 m/min at 75% efficiency; exchange rate Rs 75 per euro. Capital cost per metre, to four decimals?
The exchange rate moves from Rs 71.238 to Rs 80 per euro. The bleaching capital cost per metre becomes about:
questions.explain: 57.08 × 80 = Rs 4,566 per hour; ÷ 6,240 = Rs 0.732. Capital cost per metre moves in proportion to the exchange rate.

questions.q: Water 4,125 L/h at Rs 1, air 21 m³/h at Rs 50, steam 5,410 kg/h at Rs 0.5, power 375 kW at Rs 8; the range runs 7,800 m/h. Total utilities per metre, to three decimals?
Which single item is the largest share of the Rs 3.05 bleaching cost?
questions.explain: Chemicals are Rs 1.00 per metre, ahead of capital (0.65), water (0.53), power (0.38), steam (0.35) and air (0.13).

questions.q: In the sheet the utility costs per metre are divided by the nominal 7,800 m/h, not the effective 6,240 m/h, so if utilities keep running during stoppages they are slightly understated.
questions.explain: Capital cost uses the effective 6,240 m/h, but water, air, steam and power are divided by 7,800. Using 6,240 would raise utilities from Rs 1.39 to Rs 1.74 per metre.

questions.q: A new mercerizer raises the mercerizing cost from Rs 14 to Rs 20 per metre; bleaching 3.05, pad steam 12 and stenter 5 are unchanged. Cost of route 1?
questions.explain: 3.05 + 20 + 12 + 5 = Rs 40.05 per metre, Rs 6 more than before.

questions.q: A new stenter saves Rs 1.50 per metre on 2,000,000 m a year. At Rs 70 per euro the yearly saving is about:
questions.explain: 1.50 × 2,000,000 = Rs 3,000,000 a year; ÷ 70 = €42,857. This can be compared directly with the stenter's yearly capital cost.

questions.q: With financial cost charged at 10% of the full machine cost every year, the financial cost over the 10-year life totals:
questions.explain: 10 years × €250,000 = €2,500,000, equal to the machine price. A declining-balance method would give roughly half, so the sheet's assumption is conservative.

questions.q: Route 4 costs less than 35% of the cost of route 2.
questions.explain: 13.05 ÷ 38.05 = 0.343, i.e. 34.3%, which is why the lecture calls it a third of route 2.
